articles.title: 5 Apple CarPlay Features Android Auto Still Lacks
articles.description: While Android Auto has gained some useful features through recent updates, it still lacks many CarPlay staples that Apple users have enjoyed for a while.
articles.content:
Apple CarPlay and Android Auto lead the way when it comes to in-vehicle mobile software extensions. Each platform has gained capabilities and features since its initial release, expanding to suit drivers and their vehicle's touchscreen interface. There have been several recent Android Auto features to look forward to, including dashboard widgets and YouTube playback when parked. The tech giant has also been focusing on integrating Gemini AI more deeply into the Android Auto interface.
But Apple has been improving CarPlay along the way as well. There are quite a few CarPlay features Apple has added to vehicles recently, including its Liquid Glass design, Video AirPlay, and a new notification system. CarPlay and Android Auto do have some crossover when it comes to basic features, but Apple's continued improvements to the platform make several features unique to CarPlay users.
Because Apple puts so much emphasis on the software experience its users get across a range of devices, many of its most useful mobile features are part of the driving experience. Here we're taking a look at some CarPlay features Android Auto still lacks. Among them are some deeply integrated hands-free messaging features and a way for passengers to participate in the CarPlay experience, among several others.
Read more: 5 Things To Stop Doing If You Have A Subwoofer
Live Activities on vehicle display
Live Activities have to be one of the best iOS features implemented in CarPlay. iPhone users may already be familiar with this feature, as Live Activities come in handy in a number of different ways. The feature provides users with real-time updates from individual apps, and CarPlay presents these updates right on a vehicle's dashboard display. One of the most useful Live Activities integrated with CarPlay is turn-by-turn directions through Apple Maps.
Android Auto has a way of keeping drivers updated on tasks taking place within connected apps, though it does so in a more standard, notification-based way. The Android platform supports ongoing notifications on Android mobile devices, but Android Auto makes looking at these in detail more of a process. Food delivery apps, for example, typically run an active status tracker. Android Auto will provide notifications on such a delivery, but the specifics of it require tapping on the notification and launching the full app.
CarPlay, however, utilizes the same Live Activity interface iOS devices use. On iPhones, Live Activities will display on the lock screen and in Dynamic Island. This same interface appears on a CarPlay user's vehicle display. The CarPlay system automatically scales the interface to fit different vehicle screen sizes, but drivers can view live progress bars and real-time activity updates without having to touch their mobile device or a single button on their vehicle display's touchscreen.
Photo descriptions
Having a device read incoming text messages aloud isn't a feature that's exclusive to any one platform. It's pretty commonly used by many mobile device users, but on iOS-specific devices, when a photo is received through iMessage, Siri is capable of describing that photo. It does this with the help of Apple's Visual Look Up technology, which can identify specific objects, settings, landscapes, and more. The photo description feature is available through CarPlay, allowing drivers to get a sense of what photos are texted to them without taking their eyes off the road.
Android Auto is still not capable of this. There are some clever ways to use Gemini on Android Auto, but the ability to recognize and verbalize images through a messaging app isn't yet one of them. Gemini can summarize long texts and group chats, and even suggest replies and quick actions like sharing locations or an estimated time of arrival. But photos meant to reach a user in the midst of driving will only be announced as a photo, with the specific contents of the image needing to be checked visually once a driver is able to open the messaging app.
While CarPlay's photo description feature may initially seem like a minor convenience, it can also be looked at as a safety feature. Siri's descriptions are a legitimate reason for drivers not to take their eyes off the road when a text message arrives. Android Auto's ability to relay text-only messages to drivers eliminates the distraction in most cases, but CarPlay takes the safety factor one step further with photo descriptions.
Third-party AI chat
One of the newest features added to Apple CarPlay is the integration of third-party AI chatbots. OpenAI was one of the companies that jumped on the opportunity. With its ChatGPT app installed, drivers can hold back-and-forth voice conversations with the AI directly through the CarPlay interface. Siri was previously the only AI option within CarPlay. It's capable of handling a lot of basic assistance tasks, but expanding support to third-party AI providers opens up a lot of possibilities for CarPlay users.
Android Auto, on the other hand, limits its users to Google's Gemini AI. For years Google used its Google Assistant with Android Auto, replacing it with Gemini more recently. In a broad sense, Gemini is more capable than its predecessor, allowing for conversational interactions. But Android Auto's Gemini switch has left some drivers frustrated, and Android Auto users who'd like to turn to other AI options are unable to do so directly through the platform. Such apps can still be accessed through an Android phone, but Gemini remains the only assistant Android Auto actually integrates into a vehicle display.
While Apple at least opens the door to third-party AI integrations, CarPlay is still somewhat limited in that regard. Chatbots like ChatGPT can be accessed through a vehicle's main display, but the app's usage is limited mostly to conversational support. An app like ChatGPT isn't able to access other apps like Apple Maps, Messages, or Contacts. It's also not able to integrate with the functions of the vehicle itself. But it can be helpful for entertainment and general knowledge, as it can carry on conversations and answer questions.
Tapback message reactions
Reacting to a text message with a quick emoji, a thumbs up, or a laugh has been a basic part of iMessage for some time. CarPlay users received the ability to do this with iOS 26, which introduced the Tapback feature to the platform. In the Messages app within the CarPlay interface, drivers can select a quick reaction to an incoming text message. Previously, CarPlay users could only have Siri read the message aloud and then speak an entire response to send back.
Android Auto doesn't have a direct equivalent to Tapback, though it does have some similar functionality. The platform offers one-tap suggested replies to incoming messages, which can sometimes be as short as a quick emoji. But these are sent as new messages within the same conversation, rather than attached to the specific text they're meant to be a reaction to. CarPlay's Tapback functionality more closely resembles a mobile texting experience.
In fact, Apple's implementation of Tapback message reactions on CarPlay almost perfectly mirrors the way it works on an iPhone. Tapping a message in the CarPlay Messages app brings up the same reaction options, and drivers can even pin their most important conversations for easier access while driving. The reaction sent from CarPlay shows up attached to the original message for the recipient as well, making the messaging experience within a vehicle display nearly identical to the rest of Apple's software ecosystem.
SharePlay integration
For years, one of the major flaws of in-vehicle software platforms like CarPlay and Android Auto was that music selections had to go through the driver. When there's more than one person in the vehicle, selecting the right music for the ride required passing around an unlocked phone. Alternatively, the passengers could choose the music, requiring the driver to take their eyes off the road to manually select a track. But Apple has integrated SharePlay into CarPlay, which allows passengers to tap into the CarPlay interface with their own iPhone.
While apps like Spotify have similar features, Android Auto lacks a native equivalent to CarPlay's SharePlay integration. The Android Auto platform actually demands a third-party solution, with Spotify Jam being one of the more popular options. Passengers in an Android Auto-enabled vehicle can participate in building playlists through Spotify Jam, though it requires everyone on board to have the Spotify app installed on their mobile device. Because the feature is handled through Spotify rather than Android Auto, even iOS users could jump in.
But Apple's SharePlay offers CarPlay users a way to get in sync at the platform level. When the driver launches Apple Music in CarPlay, nearby contacts are sent lock-screen join prompts, and non-contacts can scan a QR code to join. The driver must approve all collaborators and can do so directly on their vehicle's display.

articles.title: Best VPN for Streaming 2026: 10 Top Picks Compared
articles.description: We tested the best VPN for streaming in 2026, comparing Netflix access, 4K speed, TV support, privacy, and price to help you choose the right VPN.
articles.content:
The best VPNs for streaming differ in how you unblock services and maintain playback quality. NordVPN supports major streaming platforms and fast connections, while ExpressVPN adds Smart DNS for TVs and other devices. Surfshark supports unlimited simultaneous connections, making it useful for households with several screens.
A VPN also needs to handle 4K playback, international libraries, live sports, and streaming devices without constant connection issues. Server congestion can reduce video quality, while some platforms block known VPN addresses. Smart TVs and Fire TV devices also have different setup requirements from phones and laptops.
We compared the best VPN for streaming across unblocking reliability, 4K performance, international libraries, device support, Smart DNS, privacy, and price. The 10 picks cover different streaming needs, from international Netflix libraries to live sports and multi-device households.
Best VPN for Streaming: Quick Picks
Best VPN for streaming overall is NordVPN
Best VPN for streaming on TVs and multiple devices is ExpressVPN
Best value streaming VPN for families is Surfshark
Best streaming VPN for privacy is Proton VPN
Best simple low-cost streaming VPN is Norton VPN
Best VPN for Fire TV and 4K streaming is IPVanish
Best streaming VPN for advanced users is Private Internet Access
Best VPN with streaming-optimized servers is CyberGhost
Best affordable VPN for streaming is PrivadoVPN
Best free VPN for streaming is Windscribe
Best VPNs for Streaming: Quick Comparison

Prices shown are based on the advertised plans discussed in this guide. VPN pricing varies by subscription length, introductory offers, and renewal rates, so treat these figures as a reference point rather than the final cost for every billing period.
The 10 Best VPNs for Streaming in 2026
1. NordVPN
NordVPN is our pick for most streaming setups, combining broad server coverage, strong reported speeds, and support across major devices. Up to 10 devices can be connected at once, while unlimited bandwidth gives you room to stream across phones, laptops, TVs, and other compatible devices.
Speed is particularly relevant when you are watching high-resolution content. In NordVPN’s own 1 Gbps test, downloads reached 930 Mbps, while Gizmodo’s testing, cited by NordVPN, recorded 903 Mbps downloads with a 7% reduction in upload speeds. Those results leave plenty of bandwidth for high-quality streaming without a built-in bandwidth cap getting in the way.
The server network also gives you more locations to try when you need access to different streaming libraries. NordVPN lists 7,800+ servers across 225 locations, while its apps cover Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Chrome, Firefox, and Edge. Compatible routers are supported, too, which helps when you want to connect a streaming device that does not offer a native VPN app.
Price: $3.49/month for the 2-year Basic plan, with three extra months included.
Best for: Streamers who want broad device support, high reported speeds, and plenty of server locations.
Not for: Anyone who wants the lowest monthly commitment without signing up for a longer plan.
Our analysis
We found NordVPN particularly useful when switching between streaming locations. The large server network gives you more alternatives when one connection stops working, while the reported speeds leave plenty of room for high-quality playback. The 10-device limit is the main point to watch if you plan to connect a large number of screens at home.
2. ExpressVPN
ExpressVPN is the easier pick when your streaming setup extends beyond a laptop or phone. It works across major TV platforms, streaming devices, computers, and mobile devices, so you can move between screens without changing how you use the service. The service has servers in 113 countries, giving you a wide range of locations when you need to access different regional libraries.
VPNMentor tested ExpressVPN with Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, BBC iPlayer, Hulu, Max, ESPN+, and DAZN, with HD or UHD playback reported across the major platforms tested. The same testing accessed 20+ Netflix libraries, including the US, UK, and Japan.
ExpressVPN uses its Lightway protocol for connections and supports TrustedServer technology, which runs servers entirely from RAM. The company also keeps no activity logs, while 24-hour live chat support gives you a direct way to troubleshoot connection problems.
TV compatibility is another strong point. Apple TV, Fire TV, Android TV, and Chromecast with Google TV are supported, while MediaStreamer works with selected Roku, Xbox, PlayStation, Samsung, LG, Sony, and Vizio devices. That gives you more options when your television does not support a conventional VPN app.
Price: $2.99/month on the 2-year Basic plan, with four extra months included.
Best for: Households that stream across TVs, streaming devices, phones, and computers.
Not for: Users who want extensive manual controls or a low renewal price.
Our analysis
ExpressVPN stands out when streaming happens across different types of devices. We like having dedicated options for TVs alongside the usual phone and computer apps, since moving from a laptop to the living room screen does not require a completely different setup. MediaStreamer adds flexibility, but remember that it does not provide VPN encryption.
3. Surfshark
Surfshark stands out when one VPN needs to cover an entire household. Unlimited simultaneous connections come with every plan, so you can keep phones, laptops, tablets, and TVs connected without deciding which devices get access.
Performance matters when multiple people are streaming simultaneously. Surfshark reports speeds of up to 1,615 Mbps, while its network spans 4,500+ servers across 100 countries. The servers use RAM-only infrastructure, which means stored data is wiped when a server reboots.
You also get useful tools beyond the standard kill switch. Bypasser provides split tunneling, while Dynamic MultiHop sends traffic through two VPN servers instead of one. Rotating IP goes a step further by periodically changing your IP address without disconnecting the VPN. If you already use separate antivirus protection options, the extra security tools in Surfshark’s higher tiers might not add much value.
Price: $2.49/month for Surfshark Starter on the 2-year plan, with three extra months included.
Best for: Families and households connecting many devices to one VPN.
Not for: Users who only need one or two connections and do not need unlimited-device coverage.
Our analysis
Surfshark is ideal when your VPN needs are to cover an entire household. Unlimited connections remove one of the usual headaches with family streaming, since you do not need to disconnect one device before adding another. The Starter plan also keeps the cost focused on the VPN rather than the additional security tools in the higher tiers.
4. Proton VPN
If you are looking for a streaming VPN with privacy at the center, Proton VPN takes a different approach from services built mainly around entertainment. Its free plan has no data limit, while paid plans add streaming access, higher speeds, and more server choices. That gives you a way to test the service before paying for it.
The free version connects you to servers in 10 randomly selected countries, with one device protected at a time. Upgrade to VPN Plus and you get 10 simultaneous connections, access to 20,000+ servers in 140+ countries, and support for streaming services such as Amazon Prime Video, Netflix, and Disney+.
Privacy is where Proton VPN makes its strongest case. The service says it keeps no activity logs, its apps are open source, and the kill switch protects your IP address if the VPN connection drops. Paid plans also include NetShield, which blocks ads, trackers, and malware.
Price: $3.49/month for the Proton VPN Plus 2-year plan, with a 30-day money-back guarantee.
Best for: Users who want a privacy-focused VPN with unlimited free data and the option to upgrade for streaming.
Not for: iPhone or Mac users who specifically need split tunneling, or anyone looking for reliable streaming from a free VPN.
Our analysis
Proton VPN takes a different route from the other streaming options here. We like that you can start with unlimited free data, but the free plan isn’t the best choice for reliable streaming access. The paid version changes the equation by adding streaming support, more locations, and additional connections.
5. Norton VPN
For a straightforward setup across TVs and everyday devices, Norton VPN keeps things simple. The standard plan covers up to five devices, while Norton VPN Ultimate covers 10. You can also use the service with Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Apple TV, which makes it easier to bring VPN protection to your main streaming screen.
Privacy features include a no-log policy, Kill Switch, IP Rotation, and Double VPN. Norton also includes an ad blocker, while the Ultimate tier adds broader security tools such as malware and ransomware protection, password management, dark web monitoring, and cloud backup.
Norton has also improved its performance considerably. In TechRadar’s latest testing, the VPN averaged 1,010 Mbps over WireGuard when connecting from its US test environment to the nearest Norton server. Long-distance performance remained strong, reaching 782 Mbps on a US-to-UK connection, giving Norton enough headroom for high-resolution streaming.
Price: $3.33/month with renewal options.
Best for: Streamers who want a simple VPN with support for major TV platforms.
Not for: Households that need more than five devices on the standard plan.
Our analysis
Norton VPN feels more straightforward than feature-heavy VPNs aimed at experienced users. The TV compatibility is useful if your main goal is to protect a few household screens, while the standard plan avoids bundling too many extras into the basic VPN subscription. The higher Norton tiers become more interesting when you also want antivirus, password management, or cloud storage.
6. IPVanish
Fire TV users have a particular reason to look at IPVanish. The service supports unlimited devices, along with platforms such as Netflix and ESPN+, making it practical when your streaming setup includes several screens. Its Advanced plan also includes Threat Protection Pro, which blocks malware downloads, phishing sites, and trackers.
The service offers apps for major devices and streaming platforms, while its 24/7 support is there to help when a connection or setup does not work as expected. Advanced also adds a Secure Browser, eSIM data, cloud backup, file syncing, and sharing.. Security.org recorded 93.1 Mbps on a nearby US server, 91.5 Mbps on a European server, and 90.78 Mbps on a distant Australian server from a 94.6 Mbps baseline.
You also get a 30-day money-back guarantee with both plans. The main difference between the two tiers is the additional security and storage features included with Advanced.
Price: $2.49/month for Essential on the 2-year plan.
Best for: Fire TV users and households that want unlimited device connections.
Not for: Users who only need basic VPN access and have no use for the extra Advanced features.
Our analysis
IPVanish is practical for streaming across multiple screens rather than a single personal device. Unlimited connections give it room to handle a busy household, while Fire TV support fits naturally into a living room setup. We also like that the Advanced plan includes security and storage tools, though those extras aren’t necessary if streaming is your only priority.
7. Private Internet Access
If you like having more control over how your VPN connects, Private Internet Access gives you plenty to work with. PIA gives experienced users more control over their connection, with split tunneling, protocol selection, custom DNS settings, multi-hop routing, and configurable kill-switch options. The service also supports unlimited devices, so you can use one subscription across your streaming setup.
You can choose the subscription length based on how often you use a VPN rather than paying for features you will not use. The longer plan also brings the monthly cost considerably below the monthly option.
For streaming, the appeal is less about keeping things simple and more about having greater control over your VPN connection. That distinction matters if you already know which settings you want to adjust.
Price: $2.03/month on the 3-year plan with three extra months.
Best for: Experienced VPN users who want more control over their connection settings.
Not for: Someone looking for the simplest possible streaming VPN.
Our analysis
PIA is ideal when a basic connect button does not give you enough control. Its appeal comes from the amount of configuration available, rather than from trying to make every setting invisible to the user. That makes it more suitable for someone who already knows which VPN features they want to adjust.
8. CyberGhost
Choosing a streaming server is easier when the VPN tells you which connection to use for a specific platform. CyberGhost offers dedicated streaming servers for services such as Netflix US, Netflix UK, Netflix France, BBC iPlayer, Hulu, YouTube, and Crunchyroll.
The approach is useful when you already know which streaming service you want to access. Instead of switching between several countries to find a working connection, you can select a server labeled for the platform you want to watch.
CyberGhost also gives you 7 simultaneous connections, making it practical for users who stream across several personal devices. The trade-off is its pricing structure: the lowest advertised rate requires a long-term plan, while the monthly option costs considerably
Price: $2.99/month on the 2-year + 2-month plan; $12.99 is the monthly plan.
Best for: Streamers who want dedicated servers for particular streaming platforms.
Not for: Users looking for the lowest monthly price without a long-term commitment.
Our analysis
CyberGhost approaches streaming from a practical perspective by identifying servers optimised for specific services. That saves you from guessing which location to try first, especially when you are dealing with several streaming platforms. The monthly price is harder to justify if you only need a VPN occasionally, so the subscription length matters here.
9. PrivadoVPN
A free VPN becomes more interesting when it can actually handle streaming. PrivadoVPN gives free users 10GB of data every 30 days, and its free service supports streaming at usable speeds before that allowance runs out. That makes it practical for occasional viewing rather than replacing a full-time streaming VPN.
The paid plans remove the monthly data limit and add features such as 10 connections, servers in 66 cities, streaming support, an ad blocker, unlimited devices, zero-log protection, threat prevention, and parental controls. The free allowance is the main limitation. 10GB can disappear quickly when you stream regularly, particularly at higher video quality.
Price: $1.11/month on the 24-month plan, with a 30-day money-back guarantee.
Best for: Free users who want limited streaming without a subscription.
Not for: Heavy streamers who need unlimited free data.
Our analysis
PrivadoVPN gives you an unusual way to try streaming through a free plan. The 10GB allowance is enough for occasional viewing but not regular high-quality streaming, so the free tier works better as a limited option than a permanent replacement for a paid service. The paid plans become more useful once unlimited data and additional connections matter.
10. Windscribe
Windscribe offers a free tier alongside its paid plans, giving you a way to test its VPN before committing to a subscription. The free tier is unique because it does more than offer a short trial. Windscribe gives you 10GB of VPN data every month, access to servers in 10 countries, and unlimited device connections at no cost. Its position among streaming VPNs is different from providers that focus primarily on premium subscriptions.
The free tier lowers the barrier to trying the service, although users looking for advanced features or broader coverage should look beyond the basic offering. Independent testing also gives Windscribe a stronger performance story than its free-plan positioning might suggest. Tom’s Guide recorded WireGuard speeds of 2,263 Mbps in its 2026 testing, although performance varied by server and location.
Price: The $5.75/month figure is based on its annual plan.
Best for: Users who want to test a VPN through a free tier before paying.
Not for: Power users looking for advanced features such as multi-hop or broader global coverage.
Our analysis
Windscribe is worth a look if you want to try a VPN without immediately paying for one. The free tier offers a low-risk starting point, while the paid plan removes the restrictions that become noticeable during regular use. For frequent streaming, however, the free option should be treated as a test rather than a complete long-term solution.
How We Tested the Best VPNs for Streaming
Streaming Unblocking Reliability
A VPN is only useful for streaming if it gets you past regional restrictions consistently. We assess whether each service reaches major streaming platforms and keeps the connection usable after access is established. When a platform blocks an IP address, we also look at how easily the VPN provides another workable connection.
Streaming Speed and 4K Playback
Fast download speeds look good on paper, but streaming performance tells us more. Our assessment focuses on loading times, buffering, resolution drops, and connection stability during high-quality playback. 4K video needs substantially more bandwidth than standard HD.
Netflix and International Libraries
Netflix libraries differ by country, so reaching one region does not tell us how well a VPN handles others. Multiple locations were assessed to see how consistently each service reaches international libraries. Switching between regions also gives us a clearer picture of whether you need to keep searching for a working server.
Live Sports Streaming
Sports streaming puts greater pressure on connection stability because missing a few seconds matters more during a live event. Access to major sports platforms, playback stability, and video quality throughout a broadcast all form part of the assessment. A service that works perfectly for on-demand shows still needs to prove itself when the action is happening in real time.
TV and Streaming Device Compatibility
Watching through a television often requires a different setup from streaming on a phone or laptop. Native apps, installation requirements, router support, and compatibility with Fire TV, Apple TV, Android TV, and Chromecast all factor into the comparison. Device coverage becomes especially important when your preferred streaming screen does not support a standard VPN application.
Smart DNS
Smart DNS provides another route for accessing regional content on supported devices. We look at whether a provider includes the feature, which devices support it, and how it compares with a full VPN connection. Because Smart DNS does not provide the same encryption as a VPN, the distinction matters when privacy is part of your reason for using the service.
Privacy and Security
Streaming access should not come at the expense of basic online privacy. Logging policies, encryption, kill switches, VPN protocols, and additional security tools all form part of the assessment.
Pricing and Value
A low advertised rate does not always mean a cheaper long-term subscription. Pricing was compared alongside contract length, introductory offers, renewal costs, device limits, and included features. That approach also helps distinguish the best VPN services for occasional streaming from plans designed for households with broader needs.
How to Use a VPN on Streaming Devices
Step 1: Install the VPN App
Start by checking whether your VPN offers a dedicated app for your streaming device. Fire TV, Android TV, and Apple TV support apps from several major VPN providers, so installation works much like adding any other app.
Sign in with your VPN account after installation, then choose a server location. Pick a location that matches the streaming library you want to access, rather than simply selecting the fastest-looking server.
Step 2: Connect to a Server
Open the VPN app and select a server in the country you need. For example, a US server is typically the location you would try when accessing US-based content from another region.
Once connected, open your streaming service and start playback. If the platform detects the VPN connection, switching to another server in the same country might resolve the issue.
Step 3: Use Smart DNS When Needed
Smart DNS is useful when your streaming device does not support a conventional VPN application. Instead of encrypting your entire connection, Smart DNS routes selected location-related requests through the provider’s servers. That makes it different from a full VPN and means you should not treat the two options as interchangeable.
Setup varies between providers, but you will generally receive DNS addresses from the VPN service. Enter those addresses in your device or router network settings, then restart the connection before opening your streaming app.
Step 4: Connect Through a VPN Router
A VPN-enabled router provides another option when several devices need the same connection. Once the VPN runs on the router, compatible devices connected to that network can use the VPN without individual apps. The approach works particularly well for televisions, consoles, and other hardware with limited VPN support.
Step 5: Check Your Streaming Quality
Connecting successfully does not guarantee good playback. Test the stream for buffering, resolution drops, loading delays, and connection interruptions after the VPN is active. A nearby server might deliver better performance, while another location could provide access to the library you actually need.
How to Choose the Best VPN for Streaming
For Netflix and international libraries: Prioritize a large server network with locations in the countries you actually want to access.
For 4K streaming: Look closely at connection performance rather than advertised maximum speeds alone. Stable bandwidth, low buffering, and consistent video quality matter more once you start watching high-resolution content.
For live sports: Reliability is crucial because buffering or reconnecting during a live event means missing part of the action. Look for broad regional coverage and consistently stable connections to the sports services you use.
For smart TVs: Check for native support for Apple TV, Android TV, Fire TV, or Google TV before subscribing. Smart DNS or router compatibility becomes useful when your television does not support the provider’s VPN app.
For privacy: Check the provider’s logging policy, encryption, kill switch, and security protocols alongside its streaming features. A VPN should protect your connection without requiring you to trade away basic privacy for easier access to streaming.
What to Do if Your VPN Stops Working With Streaming
Switch to Another Server
Connect to another server in the same country. Streaming platforms may block individual IP addresses rather than the entire VPN network.
Reconnect to Get a New IP Address
Disconnect from the VPN and reconnect to refresh your IP address. A new connection can sometimes bypass a temporary block.
Clear Cookies and Location Data
Clear your browser cookies and location data, then reconnect to the VPN. Old location information can sometimes interfere with regional streaming access.
Try the VPN’s Smart DNS or TV App
If you are streaming through a TV or streaming device, check whether your VPN offers Smart DNS or a dedicated app. Either option could provide a different way to access the service.
Contact the VPN’s Support Team
VPN providers often know which servers currently work with major streaming platforms. Contact support if several servers fail, especially when the VPN advertises streaming compatibility.
Final Verdict
NordVPN stands out as our best VPN for streaming if you want broad server coverage, strong reported speeds, and support across phones, computers, and other streaming devices. ExpressVPN is a strong alternative when TV compatibility matters, while Surfshark makes more sense for households connecting many devices under one subscription.
Proton VPN gives privacy-focused users a free starting point, CyberGhost offers dedicated streaming servers, and IPVanish fits households built around Fire TV and multiple screens. PIA takes a more configurable approach, while PrivadoVPN and Windscribe give you free options to test before committing to a paid plan.
Choosing among the best VPN services comes down to the streaming compromise you are least willing to make. International viewers should prioritize reliable regional access. Families need generous device limits, while 4K viewers should focus on sustained connection performance. If cost matters most, compare the full subscription price and renewal rate rather than the advertised monthly figure.
FAQs
Are free VPNs good for streaming?
Some free VPNs work for streaming, but they usually have important limits. Current testing shows services such as PrivadoVPN Free and Windscribe Free can unblock selected platforms, while data caps and limited server locations restrict how much and where you can stream.
Why do streaming services block VPNs?
Streaming services block VPNs because content licensing varies by country. VPN connections can make viewers appear to be in another region, so platforms use VPN detection and IP-address blocking to enforce regional access restrictions.
What’s the best VPN for Netflix?
NordVPN is a strong choice for Netflix streaming because of its broad server network and reported connection speeds. Access can vary by country and individual server, however, so no VPN guarantees permanent access to every Netflix library.
What’s the best VPN for Disney?
A VPN with reliable US and UK servers is useful for accessing Disney+ libraries in those regions. Current free-VPN testing found PrivadoVPN Free able to stream Disney+ through its US and UK servers, although repeated connection attempts were sometimes necessary.
What’s the best VPN for Live Sports?
The best option depends on the sports service and country you need to access. Look for a VPN with servers in the relevant region, stable connections during live playback, and enough bandwidth to maintain consistent video quality.
What’s the best free VPN for streaming?
PrivadoVPN Free is currently a strong option for free streaming, according to recent Tom’s Guide and TechRadar testing. Its 10GB monthly high-speed allowance supports selected streaming services, although that limit makes it less suitable for heavy viewing.
Will Netflix ban me if I use VPN?
Netflix can detect and block VPN connections, but a blocked connection does not necessarily mean your account will be banned. Netflix’s terms have addressed VPN use, while current VPN testing focuses primarily on whether the service can access particular libraries successfully.
Does a VPN slow down streaming?
A VPN can reduce connection speed because your traffic travels through an additional server. The impact varies by provider, server distance, network congestion, and your original connection, while quality VPNs can keep the difference small enough that streaming remains smooth.
Can I use a VPN on a smart TV?
Yes, depending on the smart TV and VPN provider. Some services offer dedicated apps for platforms such as Android TV, Google TV, and Apple TV, while Smart DNS or a VPN-enabled router provides alternatives for unsupported devices.

articles.title: OpenAI sandbox failure allows AI agent internet access
articles.description: OpenAI’s agentic AI system breached its internet-free sandbox, gaining unauthorised web access and prompting a pause in training to address security flaws. Read more at straitstimes.com.
articles.content:
OpenAI said another agentic AI system that was being trained in what was supposed to be a secured, internet-free environment was able to gain access to the web to reach an external, third-party chatbot.
The discovery was made less than a week ago, according to a blog post on OpenAI’s website on Sept 25 . One of its agentic AI systems was being trained in a sandbox environment when it exploited a “gap” to reach the public internet.
With that access, it sent at least 20 queries to an unnamed, third-party chatbot service, including “What is the capital of France”, the report showed.
OpenAI described the breakout as the first security incident of its kind since a combination of models gained internet access during internal testing and inadvertently breached the system of the AI platform Hugging Face in July.
“It gives us an important signal about where to focus the next phase of that work,” the AI developer said. The company said it decided after the latest incident to pause training with tool use on its most capable models until the sandbox flaw was resolved. “We will not resume training this particular model,” OpenAI added.
Breaches by AI models developed OpenAI, Anthropic PBC, Google’s DeepMind and Meta Platforms in recent months have alarmed cybersecurity and AI safety experts.
The Hugging Face incident was among the reasons cited by Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei when he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development two weeks ago.
His call, quickly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Elon Musk and others, has touched off a global debate over the need for more AI regulation.
OpenAI disclosed the latest sandbox failure even while it is still working to understand the disruption brought about by its agentic AI systems when they previously gained access to the internet.
The company confirmed on Sept 25 that its models accessed information from US government websites, including those of the Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission, during training and evaluation.
Just days ago, OpenAI disclosed that its models had disrupted an Australian government website earlier in 2026 .
The most recent sandbox breach also exposed gaps in OpenAI’s operational processes.
A “human reviewer” received an alert from an internal monitoring system and acknowledged it on Slack within three minutes, but the training run did not automatically stop as expected, the blog post showed.
It took more than two hours for someone to manually stop the run, according to the report.
“It’s unfortunate that even after upping their security in the wake of Hugging Face, OpenAI’s models are still capable of gaining unauthorised internet access,” said Sydney Von Arx, founder of an AI safety nonprofit Nightingale.
“The big question now is whether they will slap a Band-Aid on this and turn training back on ASAP versus if they’ll find the root cause of the issue and fix it.” BLOOMBERG
